questions.question: What are the three root categories in the MAST failure taxonomy (Cemri et al. 2025) and their measured proportions?
options: Communication failures (45%), planning errors (35%), tool failures (20%)
Specification Problems (41.77%), Coordination Failures (36.94%), Verification Gaps (21.30%)
Hallucination (60%), context overflow (25%), tool misuse (15%)
Role conflicts (50%), memory errors (30%), orchestration bugs (20%)
questions.explanation: Cemri et al. analyzed 1642 execution traces across 7 open-source MAS showing 41-86.7% failure rates. Three root categories: Specification Problems (41.77%) — role ambiguity, under-specified tasks, implicit success criteria; Coordination Failures (36.94%) — state desync, lost messages, write conflicts; Verification Gaps (21.30%) — no independent check, chain of agents each trusting the prior.

questions.question: What is a 'retry storm' and what is the standard mitigation?
options: A situation where all agents retry simultaneously after a shared timeout, overloading the message bus
A cascading failure where one service's errors trigger retries in dependent services, amplifying load exponentially until a downstream service collapses — mitigated by circuit breakers
Multiple agents sending duplicate messages to the same target due to an at-least-once queue delivery bug
An agent entering a retry loop because its verifier always returns failure, consuming tokens indefinitely
questions.explanation: The lesson's cascade example: payment fails 10% → order agent retries → each retry triggers inventory check → inventory sees 2x load → starts timing out → all orders retry inventory → inventory sees 10x load → cluster down. Circuit breaker: when downstream error rate exceeds threshold, short-circuit with cached or default results. Capped retry budgets per request also required.

questions.question: Why are verification gaps considered the most expensive failure category per incident even though they represent only 21.3% by count?
options: Verification gap failures always require human remediation, which is more expensive than automated recovery
Verification gaps produce silent correctness failures — plausible-but-wrong outputs that cannot be detected by exception logs and may propagate to downstream systems or users before discovery
The monitoring infrastructure required to detect verification gaps is more costly to build and maintain
Verification gap failures require rebuilding the entire agent system from scratch rather than patching a specific component
questions.explanation: A crash or timeout fires an alert. A verification gap does not — the system returns a confident, plausible-sounding wrong answer. Users act on it. Downstream systems ingest it. By the time it is discovered, it has propagated through multiple systems. Silent correctness failures are the most dangerous class because they are undetectable by standard monitoring without sample-based human review or golden-dataset regression.

questions.question: What are the five failure patterns in the 'Groupthink family' identified by arXiv:2508.05687?
options: Hallucination, prompt injection, context overflow, role confusion, and tool misuse
Monoculture collapse, conformity bias, deficient Theory of Mind, mixed-motive dynamics, and cascading reliability failures
Sycophancy, circular reasoning, overconfidence, catastrophic forgetting, and specification gaming
Model drift, data poisoning, reward hacking, distributional shift, and emergent deception
questions.explanation: The Groupthink family: (1) monoculture collapse — same base model shares failure modes; (2) conformity bias — agents adjust toward the loudest/most-confident peer; (3) deficient ToM — agents fail to model each other's beliefs; (4) mixed-motive dynamics — partially-aligned incentives produce compromise-middle outputs satisfying nobody; (5) cascading reliability — one component's error pattern triggers downstream error patterns.

questions.question: What is the STRATUS approach to multi-agent failure detection and what improvement did it demonstrate?
options: A new benchmark that evaluates how quickly agents detect and recover from injected failures
Three specialized agents (detection, diagnosis, validation) modeled on SRE incident response; NeurIPS 2025 reports 1.5x mitigation-success improvement
A static analysis tool that scans agent system prompts for known failure-inducing patterns before deployment
A monitoring protocol that requires all agent outputs to be checked by at least two independent verifiers
questions.explanation: STRATUS (NeurIPS 2025): deploy three agents for failure management. Detection agent: watches for symptom patterns (high disagreement, retry spikes, accuracy drift). Diagnosis agent: maps symptoms to MAST taxonomy categories. Validation agent: after mitigation applied, confirms symptoms cleared. 1.5x mitigation-success improvement from this three-agent SRE pattern applied to multi-agent systems.
